title: Truth
lead: In the Hebrew Bible truth (emet) is reliability and faithfulness, above all God's; in Greek, alētheia is what is real and not false. The Bible calls God "faithful God" (Psalm 31:5), the law says "truth is what your law is" (Psalm 119:142), and the New Testament calls Jesus "the truth" (John 14:6). 1 Esdras makes truth the winner of a contest at the Persian court.

sections.b: The Hebrew emet comes from the root of amen, "firm, sure." It is used of true words, but most often of people and above all of God, who keeps his word (Exodus 34:6; Psalm 117:2). The Greek Old Testament usually renders it alētheia, a word that in Greek leans toward what is real as opposed to false or hidden. Both senses meet in the New Testament: God's word is truth (John 17:17), Jesus is "the way, the truth and the life" (John 14:6), and the Spirit leads into all truth (John 16:13). People can swap "the truth of God for the lie" (Romans 1:25).
sections.refs: Exodus 34:6; Psalm 31:5; Psalm 117:2; John 1:14; John 14:6; John 16:13; John 17:17; Romans 1:25

sections.h: Truth in Israel's life and in Jewish tradition
sections.b: Truth in the Hebrew Bible is something to do as well as to know. "Speak truth, each of you to your neighbor," Zechariah tells the people who came back from exile, and "judge with truth and with justice that makes for peace" (Zechariah 8:16). The psalmist ties it to the law: "truth is what your law is" (Psalm 119:142). Truth and loyal love are often paired, as in "the LORD's faithfulness is forever" after "his loyal love is mighty over us" (Psalm 117:2; see Hesed). The rabbis made the word a name of God himself: Rabbi Hanina said, "The seal of the Holy One, Blessed be He, is truth [emet]" (Babylonian Talmud, Shabbat 55a).
